entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen9660" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Hymn of War and Victory in the Style of Deborah</title> <div sID="gen9661" type="x-p"/> Is it not an admirably delicate tact with which the collector makes the מזמור שׁיר <reference osisRef="Ps.68.1">Psa 68:1</reference> follow upon the מזמור שׁיר <reference osisRef="Ps.67.1">Psa 67:1</reference>? The latter began with the echo of the benediction which Moses puts into the mouth of Aaron and his sons, the former with a repetition of those memorable words in which, at the breaking up of the camp, he called upon Jahve to advance before Israel (Num 10:35). “It is in reality,” says Hitzig of Psalms 68, “no easy task to become master of this Titan.” And who would not agree with him in this remark? It is a Psalm in the style of Deborah, stalking along upon the highest pinnacle of hymnic feeling and recital; all that is most glorious in the literature of the earlier period is concentrated in it: Moses’ memorable words, Moses’ blessing, the prophecies of Balaam, the Deuteronomy, the Song of Hannah re-echo here. But over and above all this, the language is so bold and so peculiarly its own, that we meet with no less than thirteen words that do no occur anywhere else. It is so distinctly Elohimic in its impress, that the simple <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> occurs twenty-three times; but in addition to this, it is as though the whole cornucopia of divine names were poured out upon it: יהוה in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.17">Psa 68:17</reference>; אדני six times; האל twice; שׁדּי in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.15">Psa 68:15</reference>; יהּ in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.5">Psa 68:5</reference>; אדני יהוה in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.21">Psa 68:21</reference>; אלהים yh in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.19">Psa 68:19</reference>; so that this Psalm among all the Elohimic Psalms is the most resplendent. In connection with the great difficulty that is involved in it, it is no wonder that expositors, more especially the earlier expositors, should differ widely in their apprehension of it as a whole or in separate parts. This circumstance has been turned to wrong account by Ed. Reuss in his essay, “<hi type="italic">Der acht-und-sechzigste Psalm, Ein Denkmal exegetischer Noth und Kunst zu Ehren unsrer ganzen</hi> <hi type="italic">Zunft</hi>, Jena, 1851,” for the purpose of holding up to ridicule the uncertainty of Old Testament exegesis, as illustrated in this Psalm. <div eID="gen9661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9662" type="x-p"/> The Psalm is said, as Reuss ultimately decides, to have been written between the times of Alexander the Great and the Maccabees, and to give expression to the wish that the Israelites, many of whom were far removed from Palestine and scattered abroad in the wide earth, might soon be again united in their fatherland. But this apprehension rests entirely upon violence done to the exegesis, more particularly in the supposition that in v. 23 the exiles are the persons intended by those whom God will bring back. Reuss makes out those who are brought back out of Bashan to be the exiles in Syria, and those who are brought back out of the depths of the sea he makes out to be the exiles in Egypt. He knows nothing of the remarkable concurrence of the mention of the Northern tribes (including Benjamin) in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.28">Psa 68:28</reference> with the Asaphic Psalms: Judah and Benjamin, to his mind, is Judaea; and Zebulun and Naphtali, Galilee in the sense of the time after the return from exile. The “wild beast of the reed” he correctly takes to be an emblem of Egypt; but he makes use of violence in order to bring in a reference to Syria by the side of it. Nevertheless Olshausen praises the services Reuss has rendered with respect to this Psalm; but after incorporating two whole pages of the “<hi type="italic">Denkmal”</hi> in his commentary he cannot satisfy himself with the period between Alexander and the Maccabees, and by means of three considerations arrives, in this instance also, at the common refuge of the Maccabaean period, which possesses such an irresistible attraction for him. <div eID="gen9662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9663" type="x-p"/> In opposition to this transplanting of the Psalm into the time of the Maccabees we appeal to Hitzig, who is also quick-sighted enough, when there is any valid ground for it, in finding out Maccabaean Psalms. He refers the Psalm to the victorious campaign of Joram against faithless Moab, undertaking in company with Jehoshaphat. Böttcher, on the other hand, sees in it a festal hymn of triumph belonging to the time of Hezekiah, which was sung antiphonically at the great fraternizing Passover after the return home of the young king from one of his expeditions against the Assyrians, who had even at that time fortified themselves in the country east of the Jordan (Bashan). Thenius (following the example of Rödiger) holds a different view. He knows the situation so very definitely, that he thinks it high time that the discussion concerning this Psalm was brought to a close. It is a song composed to inspirit the army in the presence of the battle which Josiah undertook against Necho, and the prominent, hateful character in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.22">Psa 68:22</reference> is Pharaoh with his lofty artificial adornment of hair upon his shaven head. It is, however, well known what a memorably tragical issue for Israel that battle had; the Psalm would therefore be a memorial of the most lamentable disappointment. <div eID="gen9663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9664" type="x-p"/> All these and other recent expositors glory in hot advancing any proof whatever in support of the inscribed לדוד. And yet there are two incidents in David’s life, with regard to which the Psalm ought first of all to be accurately looked at, before we abandon this לדוד to the winds of conjecture. The first is the bringing home of the Ark of the covenant to Zion, to which, e.g., Franz Volkmar Reinhard (in vol. ii. of the Velthusen <hi type="italic">Commentationes Theol</hi>. 1795), Stier, and Hofmann refer the Psalm. But the manner in which the Psalm opens with a paraphrase of Moses’ memorable words is at once opposed to this; and also the impossibility of giving unity to the explanation of its contents by such a reference is against it. Jahve has long since taken up His abode upon the holy mountain; the poet in this Psalm, which is one of the Psalms of war and victory describes how the exalted One, who now, however, as in the days of old, rides along through the highest heavens at the head of His people, casts down all powers hostile to Him and to His people, and compels all the world to confess that the God of Israel rules from His sanctuary with invincible might.  A far more appropriate occasion is, therefore, to be found in the Syro-Ammonitish war of David, in which the Ark was taken with them by the people (<reference osisRef="2Sam.11.11">2Sa 11:11</reference>); and the hymn was not at that time first of all composed when, at the close of the war, the Ark was brought back to the holy mountain (Hengstenberg, Reinke), but when it was set in motion from thence at the head of Israel as they advanced against the confederate kings and their army (<reference osisRef="2Sam.10.6">2Sa 10:6</reference>). The war lasted into the second year, when a second campaign was obliged to be undertaken in order to bring it to an end; and this fact offers at least a second possible period for the origin of the Psalm. It is clear that in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.12-Ps.68.15">Psa 68:12-15</reference>, and still more clear that in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.20-Ps.68.24">Psa 68:20-24</reference> (and from a wider point of view, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.29-Ps.68.35">Psa 68:29-35</reference>), the victory over the hostile kings is only hoped for, and in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.25-Ps.68.28">Psa 68:25-28</reference>, therefore, the pageantry of victory is seen as it were beforehand.  It is the spirit of faith, which here celebrates beforehand the victory of Jahve, and sees in the single victory a pledge of His victory over all the nations of the earth. The theme of the Psalm, generalized beyond its immediate occasion, is the victory of the God of Israel over the world. Regarded as to the nature of its contents, the whole divides itself into two halves, vv. 2-19, 20-35, which are on the whole so distinct that the first dwells more upon the mighty deed God has wrought, the second upon the impressions it produces upon the church and upon the peoples of the earth; in both parts it is viewed now as future, now as past, inasmuch as the longing of prayer and the confidence of hope soar aloft to the height of prophecy, before which futurity lies as a fulfilled fact. The musical <hi type="italic">Sela</hi> occurs three times (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.8">Psa 68:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.20">Psa 68:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.33">Psa 68:33</reference>). These three <hi type="italic">forte</hi> passages furnish important points of view for the apprehension of the collective meaning of the Psalm. <div eID="gen9664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9665" type="x-p"/> But is David after all the author of this Psalm? The general character of the Psalm is more Asaphic than Davidic (vid., <hi type="italic">Habakkuk</hi>, S. 122). Its references to Zalmon, to Benjamin and the Northern tribes, to the song of Deborah, and in general to the Book of Judges (although not in its present form), give it an appearance of being Ephraimitish. Among the Davidic Psalms it stands entirely alone, so that criticism is quite unable to justify the לדוד. And if the words in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.68.29">Psa 68:29</reference></hi> are addressed to the king, it points to some other poet than David. But is it to a contemporary poet? The mention of the sanctuary on Zion in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.30">Psa 68:30</reference>, 36, does not exclude such an one. Only the threatening of the “wild beast of the sedge” (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.31">Psa 68:31</reference>) seems to bring us down beyond the time of David; for the inflammable material of the hostility of Egypt, which broke out into a flame in the reign of Rehoboam, was first gathering towards the end of Solomon’s reign. Still Egypt was never entirely lost sight of from the horizon of Israel; and the circumstance that it is mentioned in the first rank, where the submission of the kingdoms of this world to the God of Israel is lyrically set forth in the prophetic prospect of the future, need not astonish one even in a poet of the time of David. And does not <reference osisRef="Ps.68.28">Psa 68:28</reference> compel us to keep on this side of the division of the kingdom? It ought then to refer to the common expedition of Jehoram and Jehoshaphat against Moab (Hitzig), the indiscriminate celebration of which, however, was no suitable theme for the psalmist. <div eID="gen9665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9666" type="x-p"/> The Psalm begins with the expression of a wish that the victory of God over all His foes and the triumphant exultation of the righteous were near at hand. Ewald and Hitzig take יקום אלהים hypothetically: If God arise, He enemies will be scattered. This rendering is possible in itself so far as the syntax is concerned, but here everything conspires against it; for the futures in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.2-Ps.68.4">Psa 68:2-4</reference> form an unbroken chain; then a glance at the course of the Psalm from <reference osisRef="Ps.68.20">Psa 68:20</reference> onwards shows that the circumstances of Israel, under which the poet writes, urged forth the wish: let God arise and humble His foes; and finally the primary passage, Num 10:35, makes it clear that the futures are the language of prayer transformed into the form of the wish. In <reference osisRef="Ps.68.3">Psa 68:3</reference> the wish is addressed directly to God Himself, and therefore becomes petition. הנדּן is inflected (as <hi type="italic">vice versâ</hi> ירדף, <reference osisRef="Ps.7.6">Psa 7:6</reference>, from ירדּף) from הנּדף (like הנּתן, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.4">Jer 32:4</reference>); it is a violation of all rule in favour of the conformity of sound (cf. הקצות for הקצות, <reference osisRef="Lev.14.43">Lev 14:43</reference>, and <hi type="italic">supra</hi> on <reference osisRef="Ps.51.6">Psa 51:6</reference>) with תּנדּף, the object of which is easily supplied (<hi type="italic">dispellas, sc. hostes tuos</hi>), and is purposely omitted in order to direct attention more stedfastly to the omnipotence which to every creature is so irresistible. Like smoke, wax (דּונג, root דג, τηκ, Sanscrit <hi type="italic">tak</hi>, to shoot past, to run, Zend <hi type="italic">taḱ</hi>, whence <hi type="italic">vitaḱina</hi>, dissolving, Neo-Persic <hi type="italic">gudâchten</hi>; causative: to cause to run in different directions = to melt or smelt) is an emblem of human feebleness. As Bakiuds observes, <hi type="italic">Si creatura creaturam non fert, quomodo creatura creatoris indignantis faciem ferre possit?</hi> The wish expressed in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.4">Psa 68:4</reference> forms the obverse of the preceding. The expressions for joy are heaped up in order to describe the transcendency of the joy that will follow the release from the yoke of the enemy. לפני is expressively used in alternation with מפני in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.2">Psa 68:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.3">Psa 68:3</reference> : by the wrathful action, so to speak, that proceeds from His countenance just as the heat radiating from the fire melts the wax the foes are dispersed, whereas the righteous rejoice before His gracious countenance. <div eID="gen9666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9667" type="x-p"/> As the result of the challenge that has been now expressed in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.2-Ps.68.4">Psa 68:2-4</reference>, Elohim, going before His people, begins His march; and in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.5">Psa 68:5</reference> an appeal is made to praise Him with song, His name with the music of stringed instrument, and to make a way along which He may ride בּערבות. In view of <reference osisRef="Ps.68.34">Psa 68:34</reference> we cannot take צרבות, as do the Targum and Talmud (<hi type="italic">B. Chagiga</hi> 12 <hi type="italic">b</hi>), as a name of one of the seven heavens, a meaning to which, apart from other considerations, the verb ערב, to be effaced, confused, dark, is not an appropriate stem-word; but it must be explained according to Isa 40:3. There Jahve calls in the aid of His people, here He goes forth at the head of His people; He rides through the steppes in order to right against the enemies of His people. Not merely the historical reference assigned to the Psalm by Hitzig, but also the one adopted by ourselves, admits of allusion being made to the “steppes of Moab;” for the way to Mêdebâ, where the Syrian mercenaries of the Ammonites had encamped (<reference osisRef="1Chr.19.7">1Ch 19:7</reference>), lay through these steppes, and also the way to Rabbath Ammon (2Sa 10:7.). סלּוּ calls upon them to make a way for Him, the glorious, invincible King (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.57.14">Isa 57:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.62.10">Isa 62:10</reference>); סלל signifies to cast up, heap up or pave, viz., a raised and suitable street or highway, Symmachus katastroo'sate. He who thus rides along makes the salvation of His people His aim: “<hi type="italic">ä</hi> is His name, therefore shout with joy before Him.” The <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> in בּיהּ (Symmachus, Quinta: ἴα) is the <hi type="italic">Beth essentiae</hi>, which here, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.26.4">Isa 26:4</reference>, stands beside the subject: His name is (exists) in יה, i.e., His essential name is yh, His self-attestation, by which He makes Himself capable of being known and named, consists in His being the God of salvation, who, in the might of free grace, pervades all history. This Name is a fountain of exultant rejoicing to His people. <div eID="gen9667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9668" type="x-p"/> This Name is exemplificatively unfolded in Psa 68:6. The highly exalted One, who sits enthroned in the heaven of glory, rules in all history here below and takes an interest in the lowliest more especially, in all circumstances of their lives following after His own to succour them. He takes the place of a father to the orphan. He takes up the cause of the widow and contests it to a successful issue. Elohim is one who makes the solitary or isolated to dwell in the house; בּיתה with <hi type="italic">He locale</hi>, which just as well answers the question where? as whither? בּית, a house = family bond, is the opposite of יהיד, <hi type="italic">solitarius</hi>, recluse, Psa 25:16. Dachselt correctly renders it, <hi type="italic">in domum, h.e. familiam numerosam durabilemque eos ut patres-familias plantabit</hi>. He is further One who brings forth (out of the dungeon and out of captivity) those who are chained into abundance of prosperity. כּושׁרות, occurring only here, is a <hi type="italic">pluralet</hi>. from כּשׁר morf .tela, synonym אשׁר, to be straight, fortunate. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.68.7">Psa 68:7</reference></hi> briefly and sharply expresses the reverse side of this His humanely condescending rule among mankind. אך is here (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.9.4">Gen 9:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.11.4">Lev 11:4</reference>) restrictive or adversative (as is more frequently the case with אכן); and the preterite is the preterite of that which is an actual matter of experience. The סוררים, i.e., (not from סוּר, the apostate ones, Aquila afista'menoi, but as in <reference osisRef="Ps.66.7">Psa 66:7</reference>, from סרר) the rebellious, Symmachus ἀπειθεῖς, who were not willing to submit to the rule of so gracious a God, had ever been excluded from these proofs of favour. These must inhabit צחיחה (accusative of the object), a sun-scorched land; from צחח, to be dazzlingly bright, sunny, dried or parched up. They remain in the desert without coming into the land, which, fertilized by the waters of grace, is resplendent with a fresh verdure and with rich fruits. If the poet has before his mind in connection with this the bulk of the people delivered out of Egypt, ὧν τὰ κῶλα ἔπεσαν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμω (<reference osisRef="Heb.3.17">Heb 3:17</reference>), then the transition to what follows is much more easily effected. There is, however, no necessity for any such intermediation. The poet had the march through the desert to Canaan under the guidance of Jahve, the irresistible Conqueror, in his mind even from the beginning, and now he expressly calls to mind that marvellous divine leading in order that the present age may take heart thereat.

entries.reader_content_plain: Hymn of War and Victory in the Style of Deborah Is it not an admirably delicate tact with which the collector makes the מזמור שׁיר Psa 68:1 follow upon the מזמור שׁיר Psa 67:1 ? The latter began with the echo of the benediction which Moses puts into the mouth of Aaron and his sons, the former with a repetition of those memorable words in which, at the breaking up of the camp, he called upon Jahve to advance before Israel (Num 10:35). “It is in reality,” says Hitzig of Psalms 68, “no easy task to become master of this Titan.” And who would not agree with him in this remark? It is a Psalm in the style of Deborah, stalking along upon the highest pinnacle of hymnic feeling and recital; all that is most glorious in the literature of the earlier period is concentrated in it: Moses’ memorable words, Moses’ blessing, the prophecies of Balaam, the Deuteronomy, the Song of Hannah re-echo here. But over and above all this, the language is so bold and so peculiarly its own, that we meet with no less than thirteen words that do no occur anywhere else. It is so distinctly Elohimic in its impress, that the simple Elohim occurs twenty-three times; but in addition to this, it is as though the whole cornucopia of divine names were poured out upon it: יהוה in Psa 68:17 ; אדני six times; האל twice; שׁדּי in Psa 68:15 ; יהּ in Psa 68:5 ; אדני יהוה in Psa 68:21 ; אלהים yh in Psa 68:19 ; so that this Psalm among all the Elohimic Psalms is the most resplendent. In connection with the great difficulty that is involved in it, it is no wonder that expositors, more especially the earlier expositors, should differ widely in their apprehension of it as a whole or in separate parts. This circumstance has been turned to wrong account by Ed. Reuss in his essay, “ Der acht-und-sechzigste Psalm, Ein Denkmal exegetischer Noth und Kunst zu Ehren unsrer ganzen Zunft , Jena, 1851,” for the purpose of holding up to ridicule the uncertainty of Old Testament exegesis, as illustrated in this Psalm. The Psalm is said, as Reuss ultimately decides, to have been written between the times of Alexander the Great and the Maccabees, and to give expression to the wish that the Israelites, many of whom were far removed from Palestine and scattered abroad in the wide earth, might soon be again united in their fatherland. He knows nothing of the remarkable concurrence of the mention of the Northern tribes (including Benjamin) in Psa 68:28 with the Asaphic Psalms: Judah and Benjamin, to his mind, is Judaea; and Zebulun and Naphtali, Galilee in the sense of the time after the return from exile. The “wild beast of the reed” he correctly takes to be an emblem of Egypt; but he makes use of violence in order to bring in a reference to Syria by the side of it. Nevertheless Olshausen praises the services Reuss has rendered with respect to this Psalm; but after incorporating two whole pages of the “ Denkmal” in his commentary he cannot satisfy himself with the period between Alexander and the Maccabees, and by means of three considerations arrives, in this instance also, at the common refuge of the Maccabaean period, which possesses such an irresistible attraction for him. In opposition to this transplanting of the Psalm into the time of the Maccabees we appeal to Hitzig, who is also quick-sighted enough, when there is any valid ground for it, in finding out Maccabaean Psalms. He refers the Psalm to the victorious campaign of Joram against faithless Moab, undertaking in company with Jehoshaphat. Böttcher, on the other hand, sees in it a festal hymn of triumph belonging to the time of Hezekiah, which was sung antiphonically at the great fraternizing Passover after the return home of the young king from one of his expeditions against the Assyrians, who had even at that time fortified themselves in the country east of the Jordan (Bashan). Thenius (following the example of Rödiger) holds a different view. He knows the situation so very definitely, that he thinks it high time that the discussion concerning this Psalm was brought to a close. It is a song composed to inspirit the army in the presence of the battle which Josiah undertook against Necho, and the prominent, hateful character in Psa 68:22 is Pharaoh with his lofty artificial adornment of hair upon his shaven head. It is, however, well known what a memorably tragical issue for Israel that battle had; the Psalm would therefore be a memorial of the most lamentable disappointment. All these and other recent expositors glory in hot advancing any proof whatever in support of the inscribed לדוד. And yet there are two incidents in David’s life, with regard to which the Psalm ought first of all to be accurately looked at, before we abandon this לדוד to the winds of conjecture. The first is the bringing home of the Ark of the covenant to Zion, to which, e.g., Franz Volkmar Reinhard (in vol. ii. of the Velthusen Commentationes Theol . 1795), Stier, and Hofmann refer the Psalm. Jahve has long since taken up His abode upon the holy mountain; the poet in this Psalm, which is one of the Psalms of war and victory describes how the exalted One, who now, however, as in the days of old, rides along through the highest heavens at the head of His people, casts down all powers hostile to Him and to His people, and compels all the world to confess that the God of Israel rules from His sanctuary with invincible might. Regarded as to the nature of its contents, the whole divides itself into two halves, vv. 2-19, 20-35, which are on the whole so distinct that the first dwells more upon the mighty deed God has wrought, the second upon the impressions it produces upon the church and upon the peoples of the earth; in both parts it is viewed now as future, now as past, inasmuch as the longing of prayer and the confidence of hope soar aloft to the height of prophecy, before which futurity lies as a fulfilled fact. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.68.7-Ps.68.10">Psa 68:7-10</reference> <div eID="gen9668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9669" type="x-p"/> In Psa 68:7. the poet repeats the words of Deborah (Jdg 5:4.), and her words again go back to <reference osisRef="Deut.33.2">Deu 33:2</reference>, cf. Exo 19:15.; on the other hand, our Psalm is the original to Hab. 3. The martial verb יצא represents Elohim as, coming forth from His heavenly dwelling-place (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.21">Isa 26:21</reference>), He places Himself at the head of Israel. The stately verb צעד represents Him as He accompanies the hosts of His people with the step of a hero confident of victory; and the terrible name for the wilderness, ישׁימון, is designedly chosen in order to express the contrast between the scene of action and that which they beheld at that time. The verb to זה סיני is easily supplied; Dachselt’s rendering according to the accents is correct: <hi type="italic">hic mons Sinai</hi> (sc. <hi type="italic">in specie ita tremuit</hi>). The description fixes our attention upon Sinai as the central point of all revelations of God during the period of deliverance by the hand of Moses, as being the scene of the most gloriously of them all (vid., on Hab. p. 136f.). The majestic phenomena which proclaimed the nearness of God are distributed over the whole journeying, but most gloriously concentrated themselves at the giving of the Law of Sinai. The earth trembled throughout the extended circuit of this vast granite range, and the heavens dropped, inasmuch as the darkness of thunder clouds rested upon Sinai, pierced by incessant lightnings (Ex. 19). There, as the original passages describe it, Jahve met His people; He came from the east, His people from the west; there they found themselves together, and shaking the earth, breaking through the heavens, He gave them a pledge of the omnipotence which should henceforth defend and guide them. The poet has a purpose in view in calling Elohim in this passage “the God of Israel;” the covenant relationship of God to Israel dates from Sinai, and from this period onwards, by reason of the Tôra, He became Israel’s King (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.5">Deu 33:5</reference>). Since the statement of a fact of earlier history has preceded, and since the preterites alternate with them, the futures that follow in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.10">Psa 68:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.11">Psa 68:11</reference> are to be understood as referring to the synchronous past; but hardly so that <reference osisRef="Ps.68.10">Psa 68:10</reference> should refer to the miraculous supply of food, and more especially the rain of manna, during the journeyings through the wilderness. The giving of the Law from Sinai has a view to Israel being a settled, stationary people, and the deliverance out of the land of bondage only finds its completion in the taking and maintaining possession of the Land of Promise. Accordingly <reference osisRef="Ps.68.10">Psa 68:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.11">Psa 68:11</reference> refer to the blessing and protection of the people who had taken up their abode there. <div eID="gen9669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9670" type="x-p"/> The נחלהּ of God (<hi type="italic">genit. auctoris</hi>, as in 2 Macc. 2:4) is the land assigned by Him to Israel as an inheritance; and גּשׁם נדבות an emblem of the abundance of gifts which God has showered down upon the land since Israel took up its abode in it. נדבה is the name given to a deed and gift springing from an inward impulse, and in this instance the intensive idea of richness and superabundance is associated therewith by means of the plural; גּשׁם נדבות is a shower-like abundance of good gifts descending from above. The <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> הניף here governs a double accusative, like the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> in <reference osisRef="Prov.7.17">Pro 7:17</reference>, in so far, that is, as נחלתך is drawn to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.68.10">Psa 68:10</reference></hi>; for the accentuation, in opposition to the Targum, takes נחלתך ונלאה together: Thine inheritance and that the parched one (<hi type="italic">Waw epexeget</hi>. as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.3">1Sa 28:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.3.11">Amo 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.4.10">Amo 4:10</reference>). But this “and that” is devoid of aim; why should it not at once be read הנּלאה? The rendering of Böttcher, “Thy sickened and wearied,” is inadmissible, too, according to the present pointing; for it ought to be נחלתך or נחלתך. And with a suffix this <hi type="italic">Niphal</hi> becomes ambiguous, and more especially so in this connection, where the thought of נחלה, an inherited possession, a heritage, lies so naturally at hand. נחלתך is therefore to be drawn to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.68.10">Psa 68:10</reference></hi>, and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.68.10">Psa 68:10</reference></hi> must begin with ונלאה, as in the lxx, καὶ ἠσθένησε σὺ δὲ κατεερτίσω αὐτήν. It is true נלאה is not a hypothetical preteriet equivalent to ונלאתה; but, as is frequently the case with the anarthrous participle (Ew. §341, <hi type="italic">b</hi>), it has the value of a hypothetical clause: “and if it (Israel’s inheritance) were in a parched, exhausted condition (cf. the cognate root להה, <reference osisRef="Gen.47.13">Gen 47:13</reference>), then hast Thou always made it again firm” (<reference osisRef="Ps.8.4">Psa 8:4</reference>; Psa 15:1-5 :17), i.e., strengthened, enlivened it. But the Asaphic character of this Psalm, which is also manifest in other points, is opposed to this rendering. The description fixes our attention upon Sinai as the central point of all revelations of God during the period of deliverance by the hand of Moses, as being the scene of the most gloriously of them all (vid., on Hab. p. 136f.). The majestic phenomena which proclaimed the nearness of God are distributed over the whole journeying, but most gloriously concentrated themselves at the giving of the Law of Sinai. Since the statement of a fact of earlier history has preceded, and since the preterites alternate with them, the futures that follow in Psa 68:10 , Psa 68:11 are to be understood as referring to the synchronous past; but hardly so that Psa 68:10 should refer to the miraculous supply of food, and more especially the rain of manna, during the journeyings through the wilderness. The giving of the Law from Sinai has a view to Israel being a settled, stationary people, and the deliverance out of the land of bondage only finds its completion in the taking and maintaining possession of the Land of Promise. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.68.11-Ps.68.14">Psa 68:11-14</reference> <div eID="gen9670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9671" type="x-p"/> The futures that now follow are no longer to be understood as referring to previous history; they no longer alternate with preterites. Moreover the transition to the language of address in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.14">Psa 68:14</reference> shows that the poet here looks forth from his present time and circumstances into the future; and the introduction of the divine name אדני, after <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> has been used eleven times, is an indication of a new commencement. The prosperous condition in which God places His church by giving it the hostile powers of the world as a spoil is depicted. The noun אמר, never occurring in the genitival relationship, and never with a suffix, because the specific character of the form would be thereby obliterated, always denotes an important utterance, more particularly God’s word of promise (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.9">Psa 77:9</reference>), or His word of power (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.9">Hab 3:9</reference>), which is represented elsewhere as a mighty voice of thunder (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.34">Psa 68:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.30">Isa 30:30</reference>), or a trumpet-blast (Zec 9:14); in the present instance it is the word of power by which the Lord suddenly changes the condition of His oppressed church. The entirely new state of things which this omnipotent behest as it were conjures into existence is presented to the mind in v. 12 <hi type="italic">b</hi>: the women who proclaim the tidings of victory - a great host. Victory and triumph follow upon God’s אמר, as upon His creative יהי. The deliverance of Israel from the army of Pharaoh, the deliverance out of the hand of Jabin by the defeat of Sisera, the victory of Jephthah over the Ammonites, and the victorious single combat of David with Goliath were celebrated by singing women. God’s decisive word shall also go forth this time, and of the evangelists, like Miriam (Mirjam) and Deborah, there shall be a great host. <div eID="gen9671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9672" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ps.68.12">Psa 68:12</reference> describes the subject of this triumphant exultation. Hupfeld regards <reference osisRef="Ps.68.13-Ps.68.15">Psa 68:13-15</reference> as the song of victory itself, the fragment of an ancient triumphal ode (<hi type="italic">epinikion</hi>) reproduced here; but there is nothing standing in the way that should forbid our here regarding these verses as a direct continuation of Psa 68:12. The “hosts” are the numerous well-equipped armies which the kings of the heathen lead forth to the battle against the people of God. The unusual expression “kings of hosts” sounds very much like an ironically disparaging antithesis to the customary “Jahve of Hosts” (Böttcher). He, the Lord, interposes, and they are obliged to flee, staggering as they go, to retreat, and that, as the anadiplosis (cf. Jdg 5:7; Jdg 19:20) depicts, far away, in every direction. The <hi type="italic">fut. energicum</hi> with its <hi type="italic">ultima</hi>-accentuation gives intensity to the pictorial expression. The victors then turn homewards laden with rich spoils. נות בּית, here in a collective sense, is the wife who stays at home (Jdg 5:24) while the husband goes forth to battle. It is not: the ornament (נוה as in <reference osisRef="Jer.6.2">Jer 6:2</reference>) of the house, which Luther, with the lxx, Vulgate, and Syriac, adopts in his version,<note placement="foot">“<hi type="italic">Hausehre</hi>,” says he, is the housewife or matron as being the adornment of the house; vid., F. Dietrich, <hi type="italic">Frau und Dame</hi>, a lecture bearing upon the history of language (1864), S. 13.</note> but: the dweller or homely one (cf. נות, a dwelling-lace, <reference osisRef="Job.8.6">Job 8:6</reference>) of the house, ἡ οἰκουρός. The dividing of the spoil elsewhere belongs to the victors; what is meant here is the distribution of the portions of the spoil that have fallen to the individual victors, the further distribution of which is left for the housewife (Jdg 5:30., <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.24">2Sa 1:24</reference>). Ewald now recognises in Psa 68:14. the words of an ancient song of victory; but v. 13 <hi type="italic">b</hi> is unsuitable to introduce them. The language of address in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.14">Psa 68:14</reference> is the poet’s own, and he here describes the condition of the people who are victorious by the help of their God, and who again dwell peaceably in the land after the war. אם passes out of the hypothetical signification into the temporal, as e.g., in <reference osisRef="Job.14.14">Job 14:14</reference> (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.59.16">Psa 59:16</reference>). The lying down among the sheep-folds (שׁפתּים = משׁפּתים, cf. שׁפט, משׁפּט, the staked-in folds or pens consisting of hurdles standing two by two over against one another) is an emblem of thriving peace, which (like <reference osisRef="Ps.68.8">Psa 68:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.28">Psa 68:28</reference>) points back to Deborah’s song, Jdg 5:16, cf. Gen 49:14. Just such a time is now also before Israel, a time of peaceful prosperity enhanced by rich spoils. Everything shall glitter and gleam with silver and gold. Israel is God’s turtle-dove, <reference osisRef="Ps.74.19">Psa 74:19</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.56.1">Psa 56:1</reference>, Hos 7:11; Hos 11:11. Hence the new circumstances of ease and comfort are likened to the varied hues of a dove disporting itself in the sun. Its wings are as though overlaid with silver (נחפּה, not 3. <hi type="italic">praet,</hi> but <hi type="italic">part. fem. Niph</hi>. as predicate to כּנפי, cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.15">1Sa 4:15</reference>; Mic 4:11; Mic 1:9; Ew. §317 <hi type="italic">a</hi>), therefore like silver wings (cf. Ovid, <hi type="italic">Metam</hi>. ii. 537: <hi type="italic">Niveis argentea pennis Ales</hi>); and its pinions with gold-green, <note placement="foot">Ewald remarks, “Arabian poets also call the dove Arab. <hi type="italic">'l - wrq'â</hi>, the greenish yellow, golden gleaming one, vid., Kosegarten, <hi type="italic">Chrestom</hi>. p. 156, 5.” But this Arabic poetical word for the dove signifies rather the ash-green, whity blackish one. Nevertheless the signification greenish for the Hebrew ירקרק is established. Bartenoro, on <hi type="italic">Negaim</hi> xi. 4, calls the colour of the wings of the peacock ירקרק; and I am here reminded of what Wetzstein once told me, that, according to an Arab proverb, the surface of good coffee ought to be “like the neck of the dove,” i.e., so oily that it gleams like the eye of a peacock. A way for the transition from green to grey in <hi type="italic">aurak</hi> as the name of a colour is already, however, opened up in post-biblical Hebrew, when to frighten any one is expressed by פנים הוריק, <hi type="italic">Genesis Rabba</hi>, 47 <hi type="italic">a</hi>. The intermediate notions that of fawn colour, i.e., yellowish grey. In the Talmud the plumage of the full-grown dove is called זהוב and צהוב, <hi type="italic">Chullin</hi>, 22 <hi type="italic">b</hi>.</note> and that, as the reduplicated form implies, with the iridescent or glistening hue of the finest gold (חרוּץ, not dull, but shining gold). <div eID="gen9672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9673" type="x-p"/> Side by side with this bold simile there appears in v. 15 an equally bold but contrastive figure, which, turning a step or two backward, likewise vividly illustrates the results of their God-given victory. The suffix of בּהּ refers to the land of Israel, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.8.21">Isa 8:21</reference>; Isa 65:9. צלמום, according to the usage of the language so far as it is now preserved to us, is not a common noun: deep darkness (Targum = צלמות), it is the name of a mountain in Ephraim, the trees of which Abimelech transported in order to set fire to the tower of Shechem (Jdg 9:48.). The Talmudic literature was acquainted with a river taking its rise there, and also somewhat frequently mentions a locality bearing a similar name to that of the mountain. The mention of this mountain may in a general way be rendered intelligible by the consideration that, like Shiloh (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen 49:10</reference>), it is situated about in the centre of the Holy Land.<note placement="foot">In <hi type="italic">Tosifta Para</hi>, ch. viii., a river of the name of יורדת הצלמון is mentioned, the waters of which might not be used in preparing the water of expiation (מי חטאת), because they were dried up at the time of the war, and thereby hastened the defeat of Israel (viz., the overthrow of Barcochba). Grätz <hi type="italic">“Geschichte der Juden</hi>, iv. 157, 459f.) sees in it the <hi type="italic">Nahar Arsuf</hi>, which flows down the mountains of Ephraim past Bethar into the Mediterranean. The village of <hi type="italic">Zalmon</hi> occurs in the Mishna, <hi type="italic">Jebamoth</hi> xvi. 6, and frequently. The Jerusalem Gemara (<hi type="italic">Maaseroth</hi> i. 1) gives pre-eminence to the carob-trees of Zalmona side by side with those of Shitta and Gadara.</note> השׁליג signifies to bring forth snow, or even, like Arab. <hi type="italic">aṯlj</hi>, to become snow-white; this <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. is not a word descriptive of colour, like הלבּין. Since the protasis is בּפרשׂ, and not בּפרשׂך, תּשׁלג is intended to be impersonal (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.50.3">Psa 50:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.4.7">Amo 4:7</reference>, Mich. <reference osisRef="Ps.3.6">Psa 3:6</reference>); and the voluntative form is explained from its use in apodoses of hypothetical protases (Ges. §128, 2). It indicates the issue to which, on the supposition of the other, it must and shall come. The words are therefore to be rendered: then it snows on Zalmon; and the snowing is either an emblem of the glistening spoil that falls into their hands in such abundance, or it is a figure of the becoming white, whether from bleached bones (cf. Virgil, <hi type="italic">Aen</hi>. v. 865: <hi type="italic">albi ossibus scopuli</hi>; xii. 36: <hi type="italic">campi ossibus albent</hi>; Ovid, <hi type="italic">Fasti</hi> i. 558: <hi type="italic">humanis ossibus albet humus</hi>) or even from the naked corpses (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.19">2Sa 1:19</reference>, על־בּמותיך חלל). Whether we consider the point of comparison to lie in the spoil being abundant as the flakes of snow, and like to the dazzling snow in brilliancy, or in the white pallid corpses, at any rate בּצלמון is not equivalent to כּבצלמון, but what follows “when the Almighty scatters kings therein” is illustrated by Zalmon itself. In the one case Zalmon is represented as the battle-ground (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.110.6">Psa 110:6</reference>), in the other (which better corresponds to the nature of a wooded mountain) as a place of concealment. The protasis בפרשׂ וגו favours the latter; for פּרשׂ signifies to spread wide apart, to cause a compact whole - and the host of “the kings” is conceived of as such - to fly far asunder into many parts (Zec 2:10, cf. the <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. in <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.21">Eze 17:21</reference>). The hostile host disperses in all directions, and Zalmon glitters, as it were with snow, from the spoil that is dropped by those who flee. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.68.15-Ps.68.18">Psa 68:15-18</reference> <div eID="gen9673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9674" type="x-p"/> This victory of Israel over the kings of the Gentiles gives the poet the joyful assurance that Zion is the inaccessible dwelling-place of Elohim, the God of the heavenly hosts. The mention of Zalmon leads him to mention other mountains. He uses the mountains of Bashan as an emblem of the hostile powers east of Jordan. These stand over against the people of God, as the mighty mountains of Bashan rising in steep, only slightly flattened peaks, to little hill-like Zion. In the land on this side Jordan the limestone and chalk formation with intermingled strata of sandstone predominates; the mountains of Bashan, however, are throughout volcanic, consisting of slag, lava, and more particularly basalt (<hi type="italic">basanites</hi>), which has apparently taken its name from Bashan (Basan).<note placement="foot">This is all the more probable as Semitism has no proper word for basalt; in Syria it is called <hi type="italic">hag'ar aswad</hi>, “black stone.”</note> <div eID="gen9674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9675" type="x-p"/> As a basalt range the mountains of Bashan are conspicuous among other creations of God, and are therefore called “the mountain of Elohim:” the basalt rises in the form of a cone with the top lopped off, or even towers aloft like so many columns precipitous and rugged to sharp points; hence the mountains of Bashan are called הר גּבננּים, i.e., a mountain range (for הר, as is well known, signifies both the single eminence and the range of summits) of many peaks = a many-peaked mountain; גּבנן is an adjective like רענן, אמלל. With this boldly formed mass of rock so gloomily majestic, giving the impression of antiquity and of invincibleness, when compared with the ranges on the other side of unstable porous limestone and softer formations, more particularly with Zion, it is an emblem of the world and its powers standing over against the people of God as a threatening and seemingly invincible colossus. The poet asks these mountains of Bashan “why,” etc.? רצד is explained from the Arabic <hi type="italic">rṣd</hi>, which, in accordance with its root Arab. <hi type="italic">rṣ</hi>, signifies to cleave firmly to a place (<hi type="italic">firmiter inhaesit loco</hi>), properly used of a beast of prey couching down and lying in wait for prey, of a hunter on the catch, and of an enemy in ambush; hence then: to lie in wait for, lurk, ἐνεδρεύειν, craftily, <hi type="italic">insidiose</hi> (whence <hi type="italic">râṣid</hi>, a lier-in-wait, <hi type="italic">tarraṣṣud</hi>, an ambush), here: to regard enviously, <hi type="italic">invidiose</hi>. In Arabic, just as in this instance, it is construed as a direct transitive with an accusative of the object, whereas the original signification would lead one to look for a dative of the object (רצד ל), which does also really occur in the common Arabic. <hi type="italic">Olewejored</hi> is placed by גבננים, but what follows is not, after all, the answer: “the mountain - Elohim has chosen it as the seat of His throne,” but ההר is the object of the interrogative clause: <hi type="italic">Quare indiviose observatis, montes cacuminosi, hunc montem</hi> (δεικτικῶς: that Zion yonder), <hi type="italic">quem</hi>, etc. (an attributive clause after the determinate substantive, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.52.9">Psa 52:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.50">Psa 89:50</reference>, and many other instances, contrary to the Arabic rule of style). Now for the first time, in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.68.17">Psa 68:17</reference></hi>, follows that which is boastfully and defiantly contrasted with the proud mountains: “Jahve will also dwell for ever;” not only that Elohim has chosen Zion as the seat of His throne, it will also continue to be the seat of His throne, Jahve will continue to dwell [there] for ever. Grace is superior to nature, and the church superior to the world, powerful and majestic as this may seem to be. Zion maintains its honour over against the mountains of Bashan.

This is all the more probable as Semitism has no proper word for basalt; in Syria it is called hag'ar aswad , “black stone.” As a basalt range the mountains of Bashan are conspicuous among other creations of God, and are therefore called “the mountain of Elohim:” the basalt rises in the form of a cone with the top lopped off, or even towers aloft like so many columns precipitous and rugged to sharp points; hence the mountains of Bashan are called הר גּבננּים, i.e., a mountain range (for הר, as is well known, signifies both the single eminence and the range of summits) of many peaks = a many-peaked mountain; גּבנן is an adjective like רענן, אמלל. With this boldly formed mass of rock so gloomily majestic, giving the impression of antiquity and of invincibleness, when compared with the ranges on the other side of unstable porous limestone and softer formations, more particularly with Zion, it is an emblem of the world and its powers standing over against the people of God as a threatening and seemingly invincible colossus. Grace is superior to nature, and the church superior to the world, powerful and majestic as this may seem to be. Zion maintains its honour over against the mountains of Bashan.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.68.19-Ps.68.27">Psa 68:19-27</reference> <div eID="gen9682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9683" type="x-p"/> Now begins the second circuit of the hymn. Comforted by the majestic picture of the future that he has beheld, the poet returns to the present, in which Israel is still oppressed, but yet not forsaken by God. The translation follows the accentuation, regular and in accordance with the sense, which has been restored by Baer after Heidenheim, viz., אדני has <hi type="italic">Zarka</hi>, and יעמס לנוּ <hi type="italic">Olewejored</hi> preceded by the sub-distinctive <hi type="italic">Rebia parvum</hi>; it is therefore: <hi type="italic">Benedictus Dominator: quotidie bajulat nobis</hi>, - with which the Targum, Rashi, and Kimchi agree.<note placement="foot">According to the customary accentuation the second יום has <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi> or <hi type="italic">Olewejored</hi>, and יעמס־לנוּ, <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>. But this <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi> has the position of the accents of the <hi type="italic">Silluk</hi>-member against it; for although it does exceptionally occur that two conjunctives follow Mugrash (<hi type="italic">Accentsystem</hi>, xvii. §5), yet these cannot in any case be <hi type="italic">Mahpach sarkatum</hi> and <hi type="italic">Illui</hi>.</note> עמס, like נשׂא and סבל, unites the significations to lay a burden upon one (Zec 12:3; <reference osisRef="Isa.46.1">Isa 46:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.3">Isa 46:3</reference>), and to carry a burden; with על it signifies to lay a burden upon any one, here with ל to take up a burden for any one and to bear it for him. It is the burden or pressure of the hostile world that is meant, which the Lord day by day helps His church to bear, inasmuch as He is mighty by His strength in her who of herself is so feeble. The divine name אל, as being the subject of the sentence, is האל: God is our salvation. The music here again strikes in <hi type="italic">forte</hi>, and the same thought that is emphasized by the music in its turn, is also repeated in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.68.21">Psa 68:21</reference> </hi>with heightened expression: God is to us a God למושׁעות, who grants us help in rich abundance. The <hi type="italic">pluralet</hi>. denotes not so much the many single proofs of help, as the riches of rescuing power and grace. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.68.21">Psa 68:21</reference></hi> למּות corresponds to the לנוּ; for it is not to be construed תּוצאות למּות: Jahve’s, the Lord, are the outgoings to death (Böttcher), i.e., He can command that one shall not fall a prey to death. תוצאות, the parallel word to מושׁעות, signifies, and it is the most natural meaning, the escapings; יצא, <hi type="italic">evadere</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.41">1Sa 14:41</reference>; 2Ki 13:5; Ecc 7:18. In Jahve’s power are means of deliverance for death, i.e., even for those who are already abandoned to death. With אך a joyously assuring inference is drawn from that which God is to Israel. The parallelism of the correctly divided verse shows that ראשׁ here, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.110.6">Psa 110:6</reference>, signifies <hi type="italic">caput</hi> in the literal sense, and not in the sense of <hi type="italic">princeps</hi>. The hair-covered scalp is mentioned as a token of arrogant strength, and unhumbled and impenitent pride, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.32.42">Deu 32:42</reference>, and as the Attic koma'n directly signifies to strut along, give one’s self airs. The genitival construction is the same as in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.28.1">Isa 28:1</reference></hi>, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.32.13">Isa 32:13</reference></hi>. The form of expression refers back to Num 24:17, and so to speak inflects this primary passage very similarly to Jer 48:45. If קדקד שׂער be an object, then ראשׁ ought also to be a second object (that of the member of the body); the order of the words does not in itself forbid this (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.3.8">Psa 3:8</reference> with <reference osisRef="Deut.33.11">Deu 33:11</reference>), but would require a different arrangement in order to avoid ambiguities. <div eID="gen9683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9684" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ps.68.23">Psa 68:23</reference> the poet hears a divine utterance, or records one that he has heard: “From Bashan will I bring back, I will bring back from the eddies of the sea (from צוּל = צלל, to whiz, rattle; to whirl, eddy), i.e., the depths or abysses of the sea.” Whom? When after the destruction of Jerusalem a ship set sail for Rome with a freight of distinguished and well-formed captives before whom was the disgrace of prostitution, they all threw themselves into the sea, comforting themselves with this passage of Scripture (<hi type="italic">Gittin</hi> 57 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, cf. <hi type="italic">Echa Rabbathi</hi> 66 <hi type="italic">a</hi>). They therefore took <reference osisRef="Ps.68.23">Psa 68:23</reference> to be a promise which has Israel as its object;<note placement="foot">So also the Targum, which understands the promise to refer to the restoration of the righteous who have been eaten by wild beasts and drowned in the sea (Midrash: מבשׁן = מבין שׁני אריות); cf. also the things related from the time of the Khaliphs in Jost’s <hi type="italic">Geschichte des Judenthums</hi>, ii. 399, and Grätz' <hi type="italic">Gesch. der Juden</hi>, v. 347.</note> but the clause expressing a purpose, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.24">Psa 68:24</reference>, and the paraphrase in Amo 9:2., show that the foes of Israel are conceived of as its object. Even if these have hidden themselves in the most out-of-the-way places, God will fetch them back and make His own people the executioners of His justice upon them. The expectation is that the flight of the defeated foes will take a southernly direction, and that they will hide themselves in the primeval forests of Bashan, and still farther southward in the depths of the sea, i.e., of the Dead Sea (ים as in <reference osisRef="Isa.16.8">Isa 16:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.2">2Ch 20:2</reference>). Opposite to the hiding in the forests of the mountainous Bashan stands the hiding in the abyss of the sea, as the extreme of remoteness, that which is in itself impossible being assumed as possible. The first member of the clause expressing the purpose, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.24">Psa 68:24</reference>, becomes more easy and pleasing if we read תּרחץ (lxx, Syriac, and Vulgate, <hi type="italic">ut intingatur</hi>), according to Psa 58:11. So far as the letters are concerned, the conjecture תּחמץ (from which תמחץ, according to Chajug', is transposed), after <reference osisRef="Isa.63.1">Isa 63:1</reference>, is still more natural (Hitzig): that thy foot may redden itself in blood. This is certainly somewhat tame, and moreover מדּם would be better suited to this rendering than בּדם. As the text now stands, תּמחץ<note placement="foot">The <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi> of the first closed syllable warns one to make a proper pause upon it, in order that the guttural of the second, so apt to be slurred over, may be distinctly pronounced; cf. תּבחר, <reference osisRef="Ps.65.5">Psa 65:5</reference>; הרחיק, Psa 103:12. So also with the sibilants at the beginning of the second syllable, e.g., תּדשׁא, <reference osisRef="Gen.1.11">Gen 1:11</reference>, in accordance with which, in <reference osisRef="Gen.14.1">Gen 14:1</reference>; 53:2, we must write השׁתיתו והתעיבו.</note> is equivalent to תּמחצם (them, viz., the enemies), and רגלך בּדם is an adverbial clause (setting or plunging thy foot in blood). It is, however, also possible that מחץ is used like Arab. <hi type="italic">machaḍa</hi> (<hi type="italic">vehementer commovere</hi>): <hi type="italic">ut concutias s. agites pedem tuam in sanguine</hi>. Can it now be that in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.68.24">Psa 68:24</reference></hi> from among the number of the enemies of the one who goes about glorying in his sins, the רשׁע κατ ̓ ἐξοχήν (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">Isa 11:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.3.13">Hab 3:13</reference>, and other passages), is brought prominently forward by מנּהוּ? Hardly so; the absence of תּלק (<hi type="italic">lambat</hi>) cannot be tolerated, cf. 1Ki 21:19; 1Ki 22:38. It is more natural, with Simonis, to refer מנּהוּ back to לשׁון (a word which is usually <hi type="italic">fem</hi>., but sometimes perhaps is <hi type="italic">masc</hi>., <reference osisRef="Ps.22.16">Psa 22:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.26.28">Pro 26:28</reference>); and, since side by side with ממּנוּ only מנהוּ occurs anywhere else (Ew. §263, <hi type="italic">b</hi>), to take it in the signification <hi type="italic">pars ejus</hi> (מן from מנן = מגה, after the form גּז, חן, קץ, of the same meaning as מגה, מנת, <reference osisRef="Ps.63.11">Psa 63:11</reference>), in favour of which Hupfeld also decides. <div eID="gen9684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9685" type="x-p"/> What is now described in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.25-Ps.68.28">Psa 68:25-28</reference>, is not the rejoicing over a victory gained in the immediate past, nor the rejoicing over the earlier deliverance at the Red Sea, but Israel’s joyful celebration when it shall have experienced the avenging and redemptive work of its God and King. According to <reference osisRef="Ps.77.14">Psa 77:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.3.6">Hab 3:6</reference>, הליכות appears to be God’s march against the enemy; but what follows shows that the <hi type="italic">pompa magnifica</hi> of God is intended, after He has overcome the enemy. Israel’s festival of victory is looked upon as a triumphal procession of God Himself, the King, who governs in holiness, and has now subjugated and humbled the unholy world; בּקּדשׁ as in Psa 68:18. The rendering “in the sanctuary' is very natural in this passage, but <reference osisRef="Exod.15.11">Exo 15:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.77.14">Psa 77:14</reference>, are against it. The subject of ראוּ is all the world, more especially those of the heathen who have escaped the slaughter. The perfect signifies: they have seen, just as קדּמוּ, they have occupied the front position. Singers head the procession, after them (אחר,<note placement="foot">This אחר, according to <hi type="italic">B. Nedarim</hi> 37 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, is a so-called עטור סופרים (<hi type="italic">ablatio scribarum</hi>), the sopherim (sofrim) who watched over the faithful preservation of the text having removed the reading ואחר, so natural according to the sense, here as in <reference osisRef="Gen.18.5">Gen 18:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.24.55">Gen 24:55</reference>; Num 31:2, and marked it as not genuine.</note> an adverb as in <reference osisRef="Gen.22.13">Gen 22:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.5.1">Exo 5:1</reference>) players upon citherns and harps (נגנים, participle to נגּן), and on either side virgins with timbrels (Spanish <hi type="italic">adufe</hi>); תּופפות, apocopated <hi type="italic">part. Poel</hi> with the retension of <hi type="italic">ē</hi> (cf. שׁוקקה, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.9">Psa 107:9</reference>), from תּפף, to strike the תּף (Arab. <hi type="italic">duff</hi>). It is a retrospective reference to the song at the Sea, now again come into life, which Miriam and the women of Israel sang amidst the music of timbrels. The deliverance which is now being celebrated is the counterpart of the deliverance out of Egypt. Songs resound as in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.27">Psa 68:27</reference>, “in gatherings of the congregation (and, so to speak, in full choirs) praise ye Elohim.” מקהלות (מקהלים, <reference osisRef="Ps.26.12">Psa 26:12</reference>) is the plural to קהל (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.23">Psa 22:23</reference>), which forms none of its own (cf. post-biblical קהלּות from קהלּה). <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.68.27">Psa 68:27</reference></hi> is abridged from ברכו אדני אשׁר אתם ממקור ישראל, praise ye the Lord, ye who have Israel for your fountainhead. אדני, in accordance with the sense, has <hi type="italic">Mugrash. Israel</hi> is here the name of the patriarch, from whom as from its fountainhead the nation has spread itself abroad; cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.48.1">Isa 48:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.1">Isa 51:1</reference>, and as to the syntax ממּך, those who descend from thee, Isa 58:12. In the festive assembly all the tribes of Israel are represented by their princes. Two each from the southern and northern tribes are mentioned. Out of Benjamin was Israel’s first king, the first royal victor over the Gentiles; and in Benjamin, according to the promise (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.12">Deu 33:12</reference>) and according to the accounts of the boundaries (Jos 18:16., Jos 15:7.), lay the sanctuary of Israel. Thus, therefore, the tribe which, according both to order of birth (Gen 43:29.) and also extent of jurisdiction and numbers (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.21">1Sa 9:21</reference>), was “little,” was honoured beyond the others.<note placement="foot">Tertullian calls the Apostle Paul, with reference to his name and his Benjamitish origin, <hi type="italic">parvus Benjamin</hi>, just as Augustine calls the poetess of the <hi type="italic">Magnificat, nostra tympanistria</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen9685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9686" type="x-p"/> Judah, however, came to the throne in the person of David, and became for ever the royal tribe. Zebulun and Naphtali are the tribes highly praised in Deborah’s song of victory (Jdg 5:18, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.4.6">Psa 4:6</reference>) on account of their patriotic bravery. רדם, giving no sense when taken from the well-known verb רדם, falls back upon רדה, and is consequently equivalent to רדם (cf. <reference osisRef="Lam.1.13">Lam 1:13</reference>), subduing or ruling them; according to the sense, equivalent to רדה בם (1 Kings 5:30; 1Ki 9:23; <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.10">2Ch 8:10</reference>), like המּצלם, not “their leader up,” but ὁ ἀναγαγὼν αὐτοὺς, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.11">Isa 63:11</reference>, not = רדיהם (like עשׂיהם, ראיהם), which would signify their subduer or their subduers. The verb רדה, elsewhere to subjugate, oppress, hold down by force, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.4">Eze 34:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.25.53">Lev 25:53</reference>, is here used of the peaceful occupation of the leader who maintains the order of a stately and gorgeous procession. For the reference to the enemies, “their subduer,” is without any coherence. But to render the parallel word רגמתם “their (the enemies') stoning” (Hengstenberg, Vaihinger, and others, according to Böttcher’s <hi type="italic">“Proben”</hi>), is, to say nothing more, devoid of taste; moreover רגם does not mean to throw stones with a sling, but to stone as a judicial procedure. If we assign to the verb רגם the primary signification <hi type="italic">congerere, accumulare</hi>, after Arab. <hi type="italic">rajama</hi> VIII, and <hi type="italic">rakama</hi>, then רגמתם signifies their closely compacted band, as Jewish expositors have explained it (קהלם או קבוצם). Even if we connect רגם with רקם, <hi type="italic">variegare</hi>, or compare the proper name regem = Arab. <hi type="italic">rajm , socius</hi> (Böttcher), we arrive at much the same meaning. Hupfeld’s conjecture רגשׁתם is consequently unnecessary.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.68.28-Ps.68.35">Psa 68:28-35</reference> <div eID="gen9686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9687" type="x-p"/> The poet now looks forth beyond the domain of Israel, and describes the effects of Jahve’s deed of judgment and deliverance in the Gentile world. The language of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.68.29">Psa 68:29</reference></hi> is addressed to Israel, or rather to its king (<reference osisRef="Ps.86.16">Psa 86:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.110.2">Psa 110:2</reference>): God, to whom everything is subject, has given Israel עז, victory and power over the world. Out of the consciousness that He alone can preserve Israel upon this height of power upon which it is placed, who has placed it thereon, grows the prayer: establish (עוּזּה with וּ for <hi type="italic">ŭ</hi>, as is frequently the case, and with the accent on the <hi type="italic">ultima</hi> on account of the following <hi type="italic">Aleph</hi>, vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.6.5">Psa 6:5</reference>), Elohim, that which Thou hast wrought for us; עזז, <hi type="italic">roborare</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Prov.8.28">Pro 8:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.19">Ecc 7:19</reference>, lxx δυνάμωσον, Symmachus ἐνίσχυσον. It might also be interpreted: show Thyself powerful (cf. רוּמה, 21:14), Thou who (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.24">Isa 42:24</reference>) hast wrought for us (פּעל as in <reference osisRef="Isa.43.13">Isa 43:13</reference>, with ל, like עשׂה ל, <reference osisRef="Isa.64.3">Isa 64:3</reference>); but in the other way of taking it the prayer attaches itself more sequentially to what precedes, and <reference osisRef="Ps.62.12">Psa 62:12</reference> shows that זוּ can also represent the neuter. Hitzig has a still different rendering: the powerful divine help, which Thou hast given us; but although - instead of -ת in the <hi type="italic">stat. construct</hi>. is Ephraimitish style (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.45.5">Psa 45:5</reference>), yet עוּזּה for עז is an unknown word, and the expression “from Thy temple,” which is manifestly addressed to Elohim, shows that פּעלתּ is not the language of address to the king (according to Hitzig, to Jehoshaphat). The language of prayerful address is retained in Psa 68:30. From the words מהיכלך על ירושׁלם there is nothing to be transported to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.68.29">Psa 68:29</reference></hi> (Hupfeld); for <reference osisRef="Ps.68.30">Psa 68:30</reference> would thereby become stunted. The words together are the statement of the starting-point of the oblations belonging to יובילוּ: starting from Thy temple, which soars aloft over Jerusalem, may kings bring Thee, who sittest enthroned there in the Holy of holies, tributary gifts (שׁי as in <reference osisRef="Ps.76.12">Psa 76:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.7">Psa 18:7</reference>). In this connection (of prayer) it is the expression of the desire that the Temple may become the zenith or cynosure, and Jerusalem the metropolis, of the world. In this passage, where it introduces the seat of religious worship, the taking of מן as expressing the primary cause, “because or on account of Thy Temple” (Ewald), is not to be entertained. <div eID="gen9687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9688" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ps.68.31">Psa 68:31</reference> follows a summons, which in this instance is only the form in which the prediction clothes itself. The “beast of the reed” is not the lion, of which sojourn among the reeds is not a characteristic (although it makes its home <hi type="italic">inter arundineta Mesopotamiae, Ammianus</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.7">Psa 18:7</reference>, and in the thickets of the Jordan, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.19">Jer 49:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.44">Jer 50:44</reference>; Zec 11:3). The reed is in itself an emblem of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Isa.36.6">Isa 36:6</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.19.6">Psa 19:6</reference>), and it is therefore either the crocodile, the usual emblem of Pharaoh and of the power of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.3">Eze 29:3</reference>, cf. Psa 74:13.) that is meant, or even the hippopotamus (Egyptian <hi type="italic">p - ehe - môut</hi>), which also symbolizes Egypt in <reference osisRef="Isa.30.6">Isa 30:6</reference> (which see), and according to <reference osisRef="Job.40.21">Job 40:21</reference> is more appropriately than the crocodile (התנין אשׁר בּיּם, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Isa 27:1</reference>) called היּת קנה. Egypt appears here as the greatest and most dreaded worldly power. Elohim is to check the haughty ones who exalt themselves over Israel and Israel’s God. אבּירים, strong ones, are bulls (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.13">Psa 22:13</reference>) as an emblem of the kings; and עגלי explains itself by the <hi type="italic">genit. epexeg</hi>. עמּים .gexep: together with (<hi type="italic">Beth</hi> of the accompaniment as in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.68.31">Psa 68:31</reference></hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.13">Psa 66:13</reference>, and beside the <hi type="italic">plur. humanus</hi>, <reference osisRef="Jer.41.15">Jer 41:15</reference>) the calves, viz., the peoples, over whom those bulls rule. With the one emblem of Egypt is combined the idea of defiant self-confidence, and with the other the idea of comfortable security (vid., Jer 46:20.).
